overview.intro: The Imperial Cholas (c. 850-1279 CE) built one of the longest-ruling and most administratively sophisticated empires of Indian history. From Tanjore they ruled the Kaveri delta, sent navies to Sri Lanka and Srivijaya, and left inscriptions - above all the Uttaramerur records - that document village self-government in remarkable detail. This chapter studies their sources and kings in chronological order, their administration from the king to the village assembly, and Chola art - the Nataraja bronzes and the Brihadishwara temple.

blocks.text: The Cholas are known to Ashoka's inscriptions and to the Sangam poems, but their imperial line revives in the 9th century when Vijayalaya captured Tanjore (c. 850 CE). Fighting the Pallavas and Pandyas, Aditya I and Parantaka I extended the kingdom; after an interregnum, Rajaraja I (985-1014) created the empire - conquering Kerala, Gangavadi, northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives - and Rajendra I (1014-1044) marched an army to the Ganga and sent a fleet to Srivijaya. Chola power, sustained by temple-centred institutions and agrarian surveys, lasted, in one branch or another, until the 13th century.

Sources. Inscriptions are the primary source: thousands of Chola records on temple walls and copper plates document kings, surveys, taxes and village administration - the Uttaramerur inscriptions (919 and 921 CE, reign of Parantaka I) on the village hall wall describe the kudavolai system; the Tiruvalangadu copper plates give the dynasty's story; temple inscriptions of Tanjore record Rajaraja's endowments. The Brihadishwara temple itself is a source: its architecture, murals and inscriptions testify to royal power, wealth and piety.

Kings in chronological order. Vijayalaya (c. 850-871) - revival at Tanjore; Aditya I (871-907) - defeats the Pallava Aparajita, builds Siva temples along the Kaveri; Parantaka I (907-955) - conquers Madurai (title Maduraikonda); after a mid-century lull, Sundara Chola and Uttama Chola reign; Rajaraja I (985-1014) - conquests of Kerala, Gangavadi, northern Sri Lanka, Maldives; the Tanjore temple begun; Rajendra I (1014-1044) - completes the temple, Ganga expedition (title Gangaikonda), Srivijaya expedition (1025), new capital Gangaikondacholapuram; then Rajadhiraja I, Rajendra II, Virarajendra, Athirajendra; Kulottunga I (1070-1122) - abolishes tolls (Sungam tavirtta), restores order; later Cholas decline against the Pandyas by the 13th century.

Administration - central and provincial. The king, advised by a council of ministers (the Tiruvalangadu plates speak of a five-member council of state), headed the state. The empire was divided into mandalams (provinces, often under royal princes), valanadus, and nadus (districts), down to the village (ur). Rajaraja I's famous land survey re-measured land and fixed revenue at about one-third of produce, graded by fertility; the state kept meticulous records of land, water-rights and temple endowments. The navy and merchant fleets guarded trade; royal officers (e.g., the dandanayaka) commanded troops and provinces.

Administration - village self-government. Chola villages managed their own affairs through assemblies: the ur in ordinary villages, the sabha in Brahmadeya villages, the nagaram in trade towns. The Uttaramerur inscriptions record the kudavolai (pot-ticket) system: the sabha's members were drawn from thirty wards; each ward nominated candidates meeting strict qualifications - age 35 to 70, education in the Vedas and accounts, ownership of house and tax-paid land, honesty - and strict disqualifications (e.g., those who had served but not submitted accounts, tax defaulters, the dishonest). Names were written on tickets and drawn from a pot by lot; members served on committees (variyams) for tanks, gardens, justice, agriculture and temple affairs, for fixed terms, subject to accountings. This is India's best-documented early medieval self-government.

Chola art. Temple architecture: Rajaraja I's Brihadishwara (Rajarajeshwara) temple at Tanjore (c. 1000-1010 CE) - a UNESCO World Heritage monument - rises 66 metres in a pyramidal vimana crowned by an 80-tonne monolithic capstone, encloses a vast Nandi and shrines, and carries murals and inscriptions; Rajendra I's Gangaikondacholapuram temple and the Airavatesvara at Darasuram complete the trio of 'Great Living Chola Temples'. Bronze sculpture: the lost-wax cast Nataraja - Shiva dancing the Ananda-tandava within a flaming halo, balancing creation and destruction with serene poise - is the summit of Indian metal art, alongside graceful images of kings, queens and saints. Chola murals at Tanjore, granite dwarapalakas and temple jewellery round out a complete artistic world centred on the temple as landowner, employer, school and bank.

A bronze-casting tradition (Nataraja) that became the classical Tamil art.

questions.prompt: The Brihadishwara temple was built at:
questions.explanation: Rajaraja I's royal temple (c. 1000-1010 CE) stands at Tanjore.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing it with Rajendra's capital temple.

questions.prompt: The kudavolai system is described in the inscriptions of:
questions.explanation: The village hall wall inscriptions of 919 and 921 CE record the pot-ticket system.

questions.prompt: Rajendra I's naval expedition of 1025 CE was directed against:
questions.explanation: It secured trade routes across the Bay of Bengal.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking it targeted Sri Lanka, conquered earlier.

questions.prompt: Who revived Chola power by capturing Tanjore?
questions.explanation: He founded the imperial line of the Cholas.

questions.answer: The assembly of merchants in a Chola market town.
questions.explanation: Alongside the ur and sabha village assemblies.
questions.commonMistake: Describing it as a temple committee.

questions.prompt: Mention any two qualifications required of candidates under the kudavolai system.
questions.answer: Any two of: age between 35 and 70; education (knowledge of the Vedas/Brahmanas and accounts); ownership of a house and tax-paid land; personal honesty and no unpaid dues; those who had earlier served but failed to submit accounts were disqualified.

questions.prompt: How did Rajaraja I organise land revenue?
questions.answer: He ordered a systematic land survey measuring holdings; revenue was assessed at about one-third of produce, graded by fertility and water supply; village records kept land, water-rights and temple endowments on register, making collection systematic and audit-able.
questions.commonMistake: Saying revenue was one-half (that is Alauddin Khilji).

questions.prompt: What makes the Nataraja bronze special?
questions.answer: Cast by the lost-wax process, it shows Shiva as Lord of Dance performing the Ananda-tandava within a flaming halo - creation, preservation and destruction balanced in serene poise; it is counted the summit of Indian bronze art and a defining image of Tamil culture.
questions.commonMistake: Describing it merely as a dancing figure.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the ur and the sabha of Chola villages.
questions.answer: The ur was the general assembly of an ordinary (non-grant) village, handling everyday affairs of tanks, roads, temples and justice. The sabha was the assembly of a Brahmadeya (Brahmana-grant) village, with elaborate recorded procedure - ward-wise membership, the kudavolai draw, committees (variyams) for tanks, gardens, gold testing, agriculture and justice, and strict accounts. The sabha's records (e.g., Uttaramerur) are the most detailed; the ur was simpler and more widespread.

questions.prompt: Give reasons: the Cholas built a powerful navy.
questions.answer: Chola wealth came from overseas trade across the Bay of Bengal; the navy protected merchant fleets and ports like Nagapattinam. Conquest of Sri Lanka and Maldives required sea power, and Rajendra I's expedition against Srivijaya (1025) aimed to secure the trade route to China from piracy and rival control. The navy thus served commerce, empire and diplomacy together.

questions.prompt: Describe the local self-government of the Cholas with reference to the kudavolai system.
questions.answer: Chola villages governed themselves through assemblies: the ur in ordinary villages, the sabha in Brahmadeya villages, the nagaram in towns. The Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I's reign (919 and 921 CE) record the sabha's kudavolai (pot-ticket) system: the village was divided into thirty wards; each ward nominated candidates who met strict qualifications - age 35-70, learning in Vedas and accounts, house and tax-paid land owned, honest record - and disqualifications (unsubmitted accounts from earlier service, tax defaulters, the dishonest, those close to them). Names of qualified nominees were written on tickets and drawn from a pot; the chosen members served on committees (variyams) for tanks, gardens, gold testing, agriculture and justice for fixed terms, after submitting accounts. Tanks, temples, roads, schools and disputes were managed locally, with the state collecting revenue through surveyed assessments. This system shows accountable, educated, limited-term local administration a thousand years ago - India's best-documented early medieval self-government.
questions.commonMistake: Omitting the disqualifications or the committees.

questions.prompt: Arrange in chronological order: Rajaraja I, Vijayalaya, Rajendra I, Parantaka I.
questions.answer: Vijayalaya (c. 850) -> Parantaka I (907-955) -> Rajaraja I (985-1014) -> Rajendra I (1014-1044).
